relations.myth: Creation of the small rain ministers
relations.note: Tlaloc creates the smaller rain ministers who carry and pour his jars.
relations.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

relations.note: The Tlaloque obey Tlaloc and distribute the different waters stored in his dwelling.
relations.source: Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas

relations.note: Directional rain figures surround and pluralize the central rain power identified with Tlaloc.
Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl leads the Tlaloque and sweeps their road because wind precedes rain.
relations.source: Florentine Codex and Nahuatl lexical citations

relations.note: After Quetzalcoatl retrieves maize, the Tlaloque help release the mountain's remaining food stores.
Nanahuatl splits the food mountain before the Tlaloque seize or distribute its stores.
The Tlaloque break or blast open the food mountain and release its agricultural stores.
The Tlaloque receive, release, or distribute the personified maize stored within Tonacatepetl.
Festival language calls Chalchiuhtlicue the sister of the Tlaloque within the water-and-rain complex.
Huixtocihuatl is identified as the elder sister of the rain gods or Tlaloc complex.

relations.myth: Huemac's ballgame with the rain gods
relations.note: The Tlaloque play ball against Huemac and lose, then offer him young maize.

relations.myth: Huemac rejects the rain gods' maize
relations.note: The Tlaloque punish Huemac's rejection of maize wealth with frost, drought, and crop failure.
A Tlaloque announces the Toltec order's decline and the coming establishment of Mexica rule.
The small ritual mountain bodies are treated as Tlaloque or embodiments of their divine mountains.
The Tlaloque's rain complex shares the Templo Mayor twin pyramid with Huitzilopochtli.
